readerTitle: Why the office manager didn't pick the cheaper cleaner
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 업체, 급여 대행 업체) + 지각된 위험에 관한 연구 개념 (Bauer, 1960)
insight: 기업 고객은 '얼마나 좋은가'보다 '잘못되면 누가 책임지나'를 먼저 따진다. 그래서 가격을 깎기보다 구매자의 위험을 줄여 주는 편이 더 잘 팔린다.
misconception: 기업 구매자는 합리적이라 더 싸고 더 좋은 제안을 고른다. 거절당하면 가격을 더 낮추면 된다.

sources.text: Bauer, R. A. (1960). Consumer Behavior as Risk Taking. Proceedings of the American Marketing Association.
청소 업체와 급여 대행 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bauer(1960)가 '지각된 위험(perceived risk)' 개념을 소비자 행동 연구에 처음 소개했다는 점을 1차 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 결과 수치 없이 개념만 적었습니다.
급여 대행 사례에 법률·세무 조언으로 읽힐 내용이 없는지 확인했습니다. 특정 국가의 급여 규정은 다루지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why the office manager didn't pick the cheaper cleaner
body: Maya runs the office for a 120-person firm. Two cleaning companies bid for the contract. The new one is 15% cheaper and has glowing reviews.
She signs with the pricier, familiar one. She isn't careless with money. She's thinking about something the cheaper bid never mentioned.

image.label: Office manager comparing two cleaning quotes at her desk
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상에 앉은 관리자가 두 장의 견적서를 양손에 들고 있음. 한 장에 "$2,200", 다른 한 장에 "$2,600". 뒤쪽 창문 너머로 회의실에 손님이 들어오는 모습. 실제 회사 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: You're the cheaper cleaner.
body: You run a young commercial cleaning company. Maya liked your quote but chose the other firm. You get one more meeting.

options.feedback: You give up margin to solve a problem she doesn't have. Price was already in your favor, and a lower one can even make her worry about quality.

options.text: A one-month trial with no contract, a named supervisor, and two offices she can call
options.feedback: This costs you some effort and risk up front. In return it removes her fear that switching will blow up in her face.

options.text: Show her your eco-friendly products and better equipment
options.feedback: Nice extras, and they may matter later. But they add upside when her worry is the downside.

cards.title: The two sides of Maya's choice were not the same size.
body: If the switch works, nobody notices. If it fails, everyone knows who picked the cleaner.

breakdown.label: Best case
breakdown.detail: Saved money. A quiet line in a budget report.

breakdown.label: Worst case
breakdown.detail: Dirty restrooms before a client visit. Complaints in her inbox.

breakdown.label: Who gets blamed
breakdown.detail: The savings belong to the company. The mistake belongs to her.

cards.callout: For a business buyer, the downside is personal. The upside is shared.

cards.title: Perceived risk
body: **Perceived risk** is what a buyer fears could go wrong with a purchase, and how bad it would be. Researcher Raymond Bauer described buying as a kind of risk-taking back in 1960.
In business buying, the risk has extra layers. The product might fail. Switching might disrupt work. And the person who chose it might look bad.
So buyers often choose the option that is least likely to go wrong, not the one that is best.

image.label: A scale: savings on one side, possible blame on the other
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 왼쪽 접시에 작은 동전 더미 "Savings", 오른쪽 접시에 무거운 돌 "What if it goes wrong?". 오른쪽이 아래로 기울어 있음. 단순하고 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: Sell less risk, not just more value.
body: The sellers who win new business customers often lower the buyer's risk instead of the price:
list: **Start small:** one floor, one site, one month
**Easy exit:** no long contract until it works
**Proof from peers:** references from customers like them
**A named person:** someone who answers when things break
**A guarantee:** you pay if you miss the promise
cards.callout: Each one answers the same silent question: what happens to me if this fails?

cards.title: Risk grows with visibility and how hard it is to undo.
body: A box of pens from a new supplier is low risk. If it's bad, nobody cares and you switch next week.

Cleaning, payroll or a building's heating system are different. Everyone sees the failure, and undoing the choice takes months. The harder a decision is to reverse, the more a buyer pays to feel safe.
cards.softwareNote: Software buyers fear data loss, security gaps and painful migrations. That's why free trials, monthly plans, data export and security documents often close more deals than a new feature.

cards.title: Lowering risk has its own costs.
body: Trials and no-contract terms attract buyers who are only shopping around. Guarantees cost real money when you miss. Set limits on both.
Too much reassurance can also backfire. A pitch that is all promises and safety nets can make buyers wonder what you're worried about.
And none of this fixes a weak service. Lowering the risk of trying only helps if the trial goes well.

cards.title: Now it's payroll.
body: You run a payroll service. A 60-person manufacturer's finance manager likes your price and your reports. But her current provider has never missed a payday, and she hesitates.

options.text: Run one pay cycle alongside her current provider for free, so she can compare results before switching
options.feedback: It costs you a month of work. But her biggest fear, staff paid wrong, is tested with zero downside for her.
It makes the upside bigger, but a missed payday would still land on her. You lose margin and the fear stays.

options.text: A detailed feature comparison with her current provider
options.feedback: Useful for making the case to her boss. It shows you're better, not that switching is safe.

cards.title: Business buyers buy safety first.
body: When a business customer hesitates, the problem is rarely price. Ask what could go wrong for them, and make that smaller.
**Try it today:** list the three worst things a new customer fears about switching to you. For each, write one offer that makes it less likely or less painful.
